filing.claim: China cannot hold 4–5% growth: without lifting consumption to ~85–90% of GDP growth for a decade — which Beijing will not do — the investment-and-debt model forces a sharp slowdown. Expect 'lots of promises to rebalance but little actual rebalancing until debt levels force the issue.' (paraphrased)

where_filed.label: Carnegie — 'China Needs a Very High Consumption Share of GDP Growth' (2024)

filing.resolution: Resolves 对 (Pettis correct) if China's growth is forced sharply down — toward 2–3% — by a debt/rebalancing reckoning before 2031, absent the consumption shift he says won't come; 错 if China sustains roughly 4–5% growth through 2030 without the predicted debt-driven collapse.

audit_predictions.note: The desk's standing counter is Han Feizi, who argues the Pettis frame measures the wrong quantity — booking investment in tech and choke-point industries as waste, and treating hedonic 'deflation' as failure. On the record now; the decade will grade it.

counter.label: Han Feizi rebuts Pettis — Asia Times

filing.claim: China's external surplus does not fall as the IMF projects: the realized first-half pace (~$550B) reflects an undervalued yuan and stays elevated through 2026 rather than declining toward ~2.5% of GDP. (paraphrased)

where_filed.label: CFR — 'Time to Stop Forecasting China's Surplus Away'

filing.resolution: Resolves 对 (Setser correct) if China's full-year 2026 goods/current-account surplus holds at or above the H1 pace instead of falling to the IMF's projected level; 错 if it falls materially as the IMF forecast.

audit_predictions.note: The desk expects Setser right on the magnitude — the surplus is real and large; a fair ledger says so. The contest Han Feizi presses is interpretive: 'undervaluation/manipulation,' or the productive competitiveness and quality gains of the world's manufacturing core? Filed to grade the factual call, interpretation contested.
